newsitem.title: INDIA: New Indian government wins crucial backing.
newsitem.headline: New Indian government wins crucial backing.

text.p: India's week-old ruling coalition, shaken by a divisive corruption scandal, received a vital boost on Tuesday when former finance minister P. Chidambaram's regional party decided to join the government.

The decision by the Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) shored up Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's fledgling cabinet as it struggled to come to grips with a $280 million scandal threatening to split Gujral's party.

It also meant that Chidambaram, an outspoken advocate of economic reforms, would likely return to the government as finance minister and pilot his landmark 1997/98 (April-March) budget through parliament starting on Wednesday.

"He (Chidambaram) is a certainty," a government official told Reuters when asked if Chidambaram, finance minister in the ousted government of former prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda, would return to his post.
Financial markets had been watching keenly to see if Chidambaram, one of the architects of India's free-market reforms and a bulwark against protectionism, would return.

Share prices surged in after-hours trade on the Bombay stock exchange after the TMC announced its decision. Chidambaram and up to three other TMC members were expected to be inducted into Gujral's government this week.
The TMC is the third-largest component in the 15-party United Front coalition with 20 of the alliance's 178 deputies in the 545-member lower house of parliament.

The party dealt a blow to Gujral only hours after he was chosen United Front leader on April 19 when it decided to stay out of his government because its leader, G.K. Moopanar, had been passed over in the leadership race.
The TMC changed its mind on Tuesday. "The decision was taken in the interest of the nation and the stability of the government," Moopanar told reporters in the southern city of Madras.
"I congratulate Moopanar on the correct and wise decision taken," United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy told Reuters.
Gujral, 77, has received widespread praise for his measured approach during his first eight days in office.

But his government was caught off guard by an announcement on Sunday that federal police were to prosecute Laloo Prasad Yadav, president of Gujral's Janata Dal party and chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, and 55 others in a corruption case.
The 10 billion rupee ($280 million) scandal, stretching back more than a decade but uncovered last year, involved the alleged misuse of funds for an animal welfare scheme.
Yadav said he was the victim of a conspiracy by rightwing political opponents and bureaucrats aimed at toppling him.

"I know the real conspirators who are behind this and I will see that they bite the dust in the battle for social justice," the Press Trust of India quoted Yadav as telling party workers in Bihar's capital Patna on Tuesday.
Janata Dal leaders said senior party officials were expected to meet soon, possibly on Wednesday, to try to defuse the brewing crisis stemming from the "animal fodder" scandal.
"If he (Yadav) refuses to step down, it will make it difficult for us to run parliament and maintain public opinion," a senior United Front official said.
United Front officials said the decision by Chidambaram's party to enter the cabinet would shore up the government.
"It will boost the morale of the government," said a senior United Front leader who asked not to be identified. "The Gujral government is getting consolidated in instalments."

Gujral also received good news when the Congress party, which had provoked Deve Gowda's fall by withdrawing its vital support in parliament, announced it would not allow the new government to fall in a vote on the budget due next month.
